```{r setup}

# Packages
if (!require("pacman")) install.packages("pacman")
pacman::p_load(tidyverse,
               scales,
               ggthemes)

```

```{r data}
# A synthetic monthly revenue series with a gentle upward trend and realistic
# month-to-month variation.

set.seed(42)

# Build a trend + noise series, then rescale so the median lands at $20M
n <- 8
trend  <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)          # gentle upward slope
noise  <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.24)      # realistic variation
raw    <- trend + noise

# Rescale: shift so median = 0, scale so spread feels natural, then add $20M
raw_centered <- raw - median(raw)
revenue_raw  <- raw_centered * 5e4 + 1e5

df <- tibble(
  month   = seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = n),
  revenue = revenue_raw
)

# Quick look
# df |> mutate(revenue_M = scales::dollar(revenue / 1e3, suffix = "K"))
```

:::{style="position: relative; width: 75%; margin: 0 auto;"}

```{r chart-default}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center
#| out.width: 100%

gg <- ggplot(df, aes(x = month, y = revenue, color = "Revenue")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Revenue" = "#725496")) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "1 month") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_dollar(),
    limits = c(0, ceiling(max(df$revenue) / 20000) * 20000),
    breaks = seq(0, ceiling(max(df$revenue) / 20000) * 20000, by = 20000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title  = "Revenue by Month",
    x      = "Month",
    y      = "Revenue",
    color  = NULL
  ) +
  # worsen things up a bit by adding a gratuitous legend and plot border
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.background  = element_rect(linewidth = 0.75, color = "gray40", fill = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(10,10,10,10,"pt")
  )

gg

```

:::

## Agenda {.agenda}

1. Choosing the right chart type
2. Color and accessibility
3. Decluttering and data-ink ratio
4. Labeling and annotation
5. Common pitfalls to avoid

---

# 1. Choosing the Right Chart Type {background-color="#0f172a" color="white"}

## Match the Chart to the Question

Ask first: *what relationship am I trying to show?*

| Question type | Chart family |
|---|---|
| How does X change over time? | Line, area |
| How do parts compare to the whole? | Bar, stacked bar, waffle |
| How are two variables related? | Scatter, bubble |
| What does a distribution look like? | Histogram, boxplot, violin |
| How do categories rank? | Horizontal bar |

: {tbl-colwidths="[55,45]"}

## The Short List: Use These Most Often

- **Bar chart** — comparisons between discrete categories; always start the y-axis at zero
- **Line chart** — trends over continuous time; points imply measured values
- **Scatter plot** — relationship between two quantitative variables
- **Small multiples** — compare the same structure across subgroups

::: {.callout-tip}
**Rule of thumb:** if a table communicates it just as well, the data probably doesn't need a chart.
:::

## When to Avoid Pie Charts

- Hard to compare non-adjacent slices accurately
- Fail when there are more than ~4–5 categories
- 3-D versions add distortion with no information gain

**Prefer instead:**
- Horizontal bar chart (sorted by value)
- Waffle chart when part-of-whole framing matters

---

# 2. Color and Accessibility {background-color="#0f172a" color="white"}

## Color Has One Job Per Chart

Use color to encode **one dimension of meaning** per chart.

- **Categorical** palettes — qualitatively different groups (e.g., ColorBrewer Set2, Okabe-Ito)
- **Sequential** palettes — ordered magnitude from low to high (e.g., blues, viridis)
- **Diverging** palettes — values that pivot around a meaningful midpoint (e.g., red–white–blue)

::: {.muted}
Never use color just for decoration — it adds noise and misleads.
:::

## Accessibility First

~8% of men and ~0.5% of women have red-green color vision deficiency.

**Practical rules:**

- Prefer the **Okabe-Ito** palette or **viridis** family — both are perceptually uniform and colorblind-safe
- Redundantly encode: use **shape** or **line type** in addition to color
- Check contrast ratios for any text on colored backgrounds (WCAG AA: ≥ 4.5:1)
- Test your charts with a colorblind simulator (e.g., `colorblindr` in R, Coblis online)

## Color Don'ts

- Rainbow / jet palettes — imply ordering that isn't there; hide true gradients
- Too many categories (> 6–7 hues) — readers can't distinguish them reliably
- Low-contrast combinations — light gray on white, yellow on white
- Using red = bad / green = good without redundant encoding

---

# 3. Decluttering & Data-Ink Ratio {background-color="#0f172a" color="white"}

## Tufte's Data-Ink Principle

> *"Maximize the data-ink ratio, within reason."* — Edward Tufte

**Data ink** = ink that directly represents data values
**Non-data ink** = everything else (borders, backgrounds, grid lines, decorations)

**Goal:** every pixel should earn its place.

## The Decluttering Checklist

Remove or soften each of these unless it aids comprehension:

- [ ] Chartjunk — decorative images, 3-D effects, heavy drop shadows
- [ ] Unnecessary borders around the entire plot or legend
- [ ] Bold or dark gridlines — prefer light gray or remove entirely
- [ ] Redundant axis labels when the title already states the unit
- [ ] Duplicate legends when direct labeling is possible
- [ ] Excessive tick marks on axes

## Before / After Mental Model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Before (common defaults)**

- Dark gray plot border
- Dense gridlines every unit
- Legend floating in white box
- Axis titles in all caps
- Default font size too small
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**After (decluttered)**

- No border
- Subtle horizontal gridlines only
- Direct data labels replace legend
- Sentence-case, descriptive axis titles
- Base font bumped to ≥ 12 pt
:::
::::

---

# 4. Labeling & Annotation {background-color="#0f172a" color="white"}

## Titles Do the Heavy Lifting

A chart title should state the **finding**, not just describe the variables.

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| "Revenue by Month" | "Revenue grew 18% YoY, led by Q4" |
| "Satisfaction Score" | "Customer satisfaction dipped after the March outage" |

: {tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

## Label Hierarchy

Apply in order; stop when the chart is clear:

1. **Chart title** — the main takeaway
2. **Subtitle** — context, units, or data source
3. **Axis labels** — only when not obvious from title
4. **Direct data labels** — on bars or at line ends; eliminates need for a legend
5. **Annotations** — call out the one or two points that need explanation
6. **Caption / footnote** — data source, caveats, last updated

## Annotation Tips

- Anchor annotations to specific data points, not floating in whitespace
- Use a contrasting but restrained color (e.g., dark gray text, colored leader line)
- Less is more — annotate the *interesting* points, not every point
- In ggplot2: `annotate()`, `geom_label()`, or the `{ggtext}` / `{ggrepel}` packages

---

# 5. Common Pitfalls {background-color="#0f172a" color="white"}

## Misleading Axes

**Truncated y-axis** — starting above zero exaggerates differences in bar charts

- OK for line charts showing change over time
- Never for bar/column charts (bars encode magnitude from zero)

**Dual y-axes** — two different scales on one chart almost always mislead

- Use small multiples instead, or pick the more important variable

## Overplotting and Clutter

- **Too many series** on one line chart → spaghetti; use small multiples or highlight one
- **Overlapping points** in scatter plots → use `alpha` transparency, jitter, or 2-D density
- **Too much data** in one view → filter to the most relevant slice, let users drill down

## Chartjunk Hall of Shame

- 3-D bar/pie charts — perspective distorts perceived area
- Exploding pie charts — emphasizes a slice arbitrarily
- Gradient fills — suggest a data dimension that isn't there
- Stock photo backgrounds — compete with the data
- Clip art / icons replacing bars — imprecise and distracting

## The Publication Checklist

Before sharing any chart, verify:

- [ ] Title states the finding
- [ ] Axes start at appropriate baselines; labeled with units
- [ ] Color is purposeful and colorblind-safe
- [ ] No unnecessary chartjunk
- [ ] Source and date noted in caption
- [ ] Legible at the intended output size

---

# Summary {background-color="#0f172a" color="white"}

## Five Principles to Remember

1. **Right chart** — match the visual form to the question being answered
2. **Purposeful color** — one encoding per chart, always accessible
3. **Data-ink ratio** — remove anything that doesn't carry information
4. **Honest labeling** — titles that state findings; axes that don't mislead
5. **Intentional annotation** — guide the reader's eye to what matters

::: {.callout-tip}
The best visualization is the one that lets the data speak without getting in the way.
:::
